We release the site in two steps. First, we upload all the new assets under versioned filenames, such as `app.v2.js`. Once every new file is available, we switch the manifest to point to those filenames. The upload comes first so a browser that fetches the new manifest can immediately load every file it references. Switching earlier could send a browser to a file that still hasn’t been uploaded, causing a 404.

We keep the old assets because a browser can fetch a manifest and request its files at different times. A tab that fetched the previous manifest just before the switch might request `app.v1.js` just after it. Keeping that file at its original URL lets the tab finish loading the version it started with.

The manifest tells browsers which asset names to request. We upload all new assets under versioned names before switching the manifest so every file it lists is already available when a browser requests it.

We keep the old assets because a browser that fetched the previous manifest can still request a file by its old name after the switch. Keeping that file available lets the browser finish loading the previous release.

Think of the manifest as a list of filenames the browser should load. We upload every new asset under its versioned name before switching the manifest. That way, as soon as a browser fetches the new manifest, every file it asks for is already available. Switching earlier could leave a browser requesting a file that’s still uploading and getting a 404.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn’t update the copy a browser already fetched. A tab opened before the release might request a script later, when someone opens a feature for the first time. That tab will use the old filename. Keeping the file available lets the feature load even after the new release goes live.
